text.p: CompUSA Inc Chief Executive Officer Jim Halpin said the company's retail sales had been "somewhat sluggish" and he was looking ahead to the holiday selling season with only "cautious optimism."

Halpin said the Dallas-based retailer had an excellent fiscal first quarter, ended September 28, and that other areas of its business were doing well. But he indicated that the growth of retail sales had slowed.
"Overall, retail sales have been somewhat sluggish," he said on a conference call. "Like all retailers, we are approaching the holiday season with cautious optimism."
Halpin said CompUSA's direct sales to corporations and its services business were doing well and were helping to make up for the slower retail business.
"Fortunately, CompUSA's operating model is not totally dependent on any one of our seven businesses," he said.

"For the last 12 months, the trend has been that our corporate and services businesses have grown at a faster rate than our retail business. Because of a wide range of opportunities in both direct and service segments, we believe that this trend will continue," he said.

CompUSA today reported first quarter (ended September 28) earnings of $14.5 million, or $0.31 per share, up from $6.2 million, or $0.15 per share, in the same period last year. Revenues were up 26.7 percent to $991 million.
The company also said same-store sales, taken from the 86 stores open for one year or more, were up 7.2 percent in the first quarter.
Halpin said CompUSA has opened five new stores so far in the second quarter and will open another nine before the quarter ends.

Despite the stronger-than-expected first quarter results, CompUSA's stock was down five points at 46-1/2 on the New York Stock Exchange. The shares fell 5-1/2 on Tuesday after Salomon Brothers warned of a softening of retail computer sales.
Halpin said he had seen some improvement in sales of Apple Computer Inc products.

Lawrence Mondry, CompUSA executive vice president for marketing, said consumer demand during the upcoming holiday season could be stimulated by the release of new products and aggressive marketing by manufacturers.
Mondry said notebooks "continue to be very, very strong," and he forecast that the 200-megahertz Pentium desktop personal computers would sell very well.
He said laptop computers would continue to sell well and predicted that new hand-held personal computers and personal digital assistance products would become very popular.
